#152036. Latest Update: 10 Best Meal Delivery Services, Tested by an Ex-Restaurant Critic

📅 01 Feb 2020 • ⏱️ 39m • 📚 Deep Dive (7844 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 10 Best Meal Delivery Services, Tested by an Ex-Restaurant Critic

📅 01 Feb 2020 | ⏱️ 39 min read (7844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~39 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meal delivery services and meal kits make your home life easier—and maybe make dinner something to look forward to rather than dread.
  • Recent findings suggest that the best meal kits help you climb out of a cooking rut of turning to the same dishes—and the same flavors—over and over.
  • Recent findings suggest that but depending on your priorities, other meal delivery services might be a better option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meal delivery services and meal kits make your home life easier—and maybe make dinner something to look forward to rather than dread. Our lead tester for this guide, former WIRED Reviews writer Matthew Korfhage, didn’t expect to appreciate meal kits as much as he did, especially since he likes to cook and worked as a food critic on both coasts for more than a decade.

Recent findings suggest that the best meal kits help you climb out of a cooking rut of turning to the same dishes—and the same flavors—over and over. After testing every major meal delivery service over the past two years, we’ve narrowed the field to just a few of the best options for each family and diet. Quite simply, the best meals our testers have eaten from a meal kit come from Marley Spoon, which offers a path to genuinely good home-cooked meals on nights when you might otherwise feel uninspired.

Recent findings suggest that but depending on your priorities, other meal delivery services might be a better option. Home Chef offers the greatest flexibility for busy families while keeping prices affordable. EveryPlate is the best meal kit for people on a tight budget. For a healthful, tailored diet (including an option for true gluten-free meals), we recommend Green Chef. If you’d rather not cook at all, CookUnity is the best prepared-meal delivery service we’ve ever had the pleasure to warm up.

We assessed each meal proposal’s recipes, variety, sourcing, ease of preparation, convenience, organization, packaging, ingredient quality, and suitability for different dietary restrictions and needs. We also tested the best new and innovative meal kits for those looking for alternatives to Blue Apron's or HelloFresh’s long-standing meal delivery services. And not for nothing, we sorted out some often maddeningly nontransparent pricing.

Be sure to check out our investigation into whether meal kits are sometimes cheaper than groceries when trying out latest recipes, and WIRED's related guides, including Best Plant-Based Meal Kits, Best Food Gifts You Can Buy Online, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Delivery Chocolate Boxes.

Updated November 2026: We’re retesting the kits in this guide, including special holiday offerings from meal kit makers like Marley Spoon. We’ve added some notes reflecting this in relevant sections and checked for accuracy throughout.

In the decade since it was introduced on American shores, the strength of the Martha Stewart–endorsed Marley Spoon meal delivery service has remained steadfast: It’s the cooking.

The best individual meals we’ve cooked from the 20 or so kits we’ve tested over the past two years have come from Marley Spoon. A hearty, Hungarian-influenced creamy mushroom chicken; a boldly Cajun-spiced whitefish; or a delicate eggplant parm. Those meals are still on the menu.

But Marley Spoon has also been evolving of late. Over the past year or two, the German-founded meal kit has added more menu items, more cosmopolitan meals with global flavors, and a greater variety of preparation times that now include a lot of 15-minute meals. It’s done this without raising the price of the meal kit this year—no mean feat amid rising food and shipping costs.

The classic “Martha’s Best” recipes are now augmented by meals that emphasize convenience and global flavors. A third of the menu is now prepared, ready-to-heat meals. There are more 15-minute dishes and tray oven bakes. Marley Spoon also seems to have broadened its international fare, with takes on a Moroccan-spiced apricot and beef tagine and Indian-influenced keema matar that’s as easy to make as garam masala sloppy Joe. You can even get special holiday kits—we can confirm that the Thanksgiving feasts are excellent, and more specialty meal options abound for December holidays.

Still, more than other meal kits, Marley remains devoted to classical cooking technique—the sort they teach in culinary school and on Martha Stewart’s TV highlights. This is no accident. When the German-founded meal kit arrived in the US, it did so with the cooking maven’s endorsement and a lot of her recipes and techniques. Recipes often call for light seasoning throughout the process—not all at once. A deeply savory kale and sausage soup might be balanced with acid from a surprising splash of red wine vinegar.

Recent findings suggest that marley Spoon is more honest than most meal kits about the time it actually takes to cook a recipe. While your 15-minute meal might acccctually still require 20 minutes, it definitely won’t take 30 or 40. There is one point of inconvenience with Marley, one that might help keep the company’s prices from climbing: Unlike other top-line kits, Marley sends your ingredients jumbled in a box, which reduces packaging waste but also leaves you hunting for the right spice mix or dried ingredient. The meat sourcing also isn’t as transparent as in some kits.

Industry observers note that like Blue Apron and others, Marley Spoon has recently partnered with food delivery service Misfits Market after its previous US partner, FreshRealm, filed for Chapter 11 protection. We'll be testing and monitoring to make sure Marley keeps earning its spot at the top of this list. While maintaining value, Marley Spoon offers genuinely good cooking and acts as a little school in culinary techniques. Some other meal kits on this list might offer more flexibility. Marley offers a firm backbone.

It has been revealed that home Chef lets you do pretty much whatever you want. Do you want two servings of two recipes, but eight servings of a third? No problem. Did you want to add an oven-ready steak meal for six to this week’s order, and only this week’s order? Also not a problem. Have a large family? Home Chef offers a cheaper family blueprint for batched family meals. Want fewer meals this week than your typical order? Each meal will cost a little more, but you can still cut back your order on the fly without canceling.

More than any other meal kit we’ve tested, Home Chef is optimized for convenience, down to the transparent plastic bags that house each meal’s ingredients. The recipes are finely detailed, with easy-to-follow instructions. Nutrition and allergens are listed in even finer detail online. Each recipe is classed according to difficulty, and even the theoretically highfalutin’ “culinary collection” meals aren’t hard to make or dauntingly culinary—mayhaps a stuffed chicken breast, perhaps some gnocchi.

According to recent reports, it’s no surprise that WIRED previously listed Home Chef as the best meal kit for beginner chefs: the recipe instructions are full of little hand-holds and extra advice. That said, the meals we tried weren’t quite as sophisticated or as tasty as those from our top pick, Marley Spoon, nor as varied and interesting as HelloFresh. One “culinary” meal was basically a stuffed burger with seasoned fries.

It has been revealed that but convenience, flexibility, and good administration count for a lot in this world. So do relatively low prices: $10 a meal on most standard plans and $8 a plate on the kid-friendly family plan. If you’ve got a family life with meal demands that change from week to week—which is what a lot of people looking to meal kits are trying to solve—Home Chef may be the meal kit you need.

Recent findings suggest that cookUnity is the only prepared-meal delivery service we’ve tried that has ever delivered a meal better than local restaurant takeout. Specifically, from the Seattle kitchen run by chef Gaurav Raj, former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tried multiple Indian gravies, from butter chicken to chicken lababdar, that tasted better than what he could get at the Punjabi restaurant down the street.

Prepared meal delivery services promise a hunger-squelching holy grail: fresh meals, delivered to your door in a box that’s ready to heat and eat, minus all the effort of actually cooking it. But the results from many other prepared-meal delivery services have been mixed. Indeed, some struggle to better the TV dinners they resemble. The reason CookUnity has been a major standout is its unique business model.

In a recent development, most prepared meal aims come from a single significant corporate kitchen. But CookUnity is more like a cross between a meal service and DoorDash. CookUnity enlists restaurant chefs, often big names like Jose Garces or Rick Bayless or Iron Chef contestants, to design recipes and hire cooks who make your meals out of regional commissary kitchens, and ship them never-frozen down the street. This model leads not just to quality but also to diversity of food.

Over two years of testing, we’ve tried multiple well-composed salads, a surprisingly wonderful truffled beef stroganoff, credible Filipino adobo, and Japanese-style katsu with curry that crisped up tantalizingly in an air fryer.

According to recent reports, menus, chefs, and (probably) results may vary depending on your region and your distance from the cooking hub. Hubs now include New York, Austin, Miami, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Seattle, Chicago, and Toronto. (See the delivery map to check whether CookUnity services your area.) Korfhage had good results from the small Seattle hub, and WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe noted the adobo flank steak and rigatoni alla vodka she scored from the Chicago hub straight-up blew her mind.

Prep tends to happen one of two ways: either you nuke it, or you follow the chef’s ideal stovetop or oven instructions to create optimal texture and flavor. After reheating, you might also stretch burrata cheese over your pasta or ladle cumin-forward sauce on your salmon. The meals are filling, the textures are spot-on, and the packaging is compostable and recyclable. Each meal lasts in the fridge between four and seven days from the date of delivery, through the miracle of modified atmosphere packaging.

After retesting CookUnity this year during warmer weather in Oregon, we found that meals arrived at food-safe temperatures—no small feat, given that some meals drove in from four hours away.

Sources indicate that helloFresh is pretty much synonymous with “meal kits.” It’s the biggest and one of the oldest services. It’s become a global brand, available in 18 countries. Chances are, if you’ve tried a meal kit, it’s one of the first you tried. What’s surprised us, though, is how much HelloFresh has improved since we first tried it: better sourcing and more cosmopolitan, modern recipes.

It has been revealed that the brand has become a logistics powerhouse. These days, you get seasonal or even regional ingredients, depending on where you live. Proteins are sourced from multigenerational, family-run meat purveyors. Each subscription box is also well-organized, with each recipe’s ingredients portioned into labeled bags. All you need are pots, pans, a stove, and basic oil, salt, and butter.

In a recent development, especially over the past year, HelloFresh has undergone a near-astonishing expansion of its menu. Where Korfhage lives, more than 400 menu items are available each week, spanning a truly global range of cuisines. One day, he could find himself deep in a Gambian-inspired peanut stew. The next it’s an aspirational Hainanese chicken feast, a simplified Thai-style green curry shrimp, Tex-Mex enchiladas slathered in cheese and ranchero sauce, or Guamanian-inflected chicken kelaguen. Or he can just make himself a salad, wrap, or sandwich.

This summer, HelloFresh has even offered single-order grill boxes in partnership with meat delivery service Good Chop, with 32 servings comprising burgers (six), dogs (eight), steaks (four), sausages (eight), and bacon (eight strips) for $80. (According to Korfhage, the steaks and bacon were the two best-selling points.).

Where possible, HelloFresh has even begun dabbling in seasonal ingredients, like conehead cabbage Korfhage charred on his grill last summer. In some areas, HelloFresh has even added regional dishes and ingredients. It’s an exercise in logistics that makes the home chefs a little giddy. After criticism, the tech giant added more rice to the rice meals last year. That remarked, shipping prices are up, and the per-serving price has also hiked around 50 cents this year—a tribute to the rising gas and food prices that have plagued 2026.

The global offerings don’t make much claim to authenticity, mind you. Also, HelloFresh’s 20-minute meals sometimes take as long as 40 minutes to make. But HelloFresh’s offerings look a lot like how people eat these days. They are bright, light, and lightly internationalized: with pan-Latin steak and rice bowls, beef stir-fried with ponzu and plum, Dutch-inspired orange Dijon chicken, Thai-style curries, and maybe some mango salsa atop a vaguely Southwest-y pork roast.

Green Chef is first and foremost the organic arm of HelloFresh, assiduous enough that they sent an apology note when they had to sub in nonorganic Roma tomatoes. In a recent August test, Green Chef’s fresh ingredients and sourcing impressed as much as any meal kit we’ve tasted, including fresh herbs, seasonal fare, wild-caught sockeye salmon, and delicious (farmed) steelhead trout.

The healthiest diet is the one that’s attentive to your specific needs, and this is where Green Chef shines. The meal program has a strong vegetarian and dairy-free focus and at least 10 keto meals a week. Green Chef is also among the few meal delivery services that prepare its gluten-free meals in separate facilities—backed by independent validation from the Seattle-area Gluten Intolerance Group. As of August, more than half of Green Chef's meals are gluten-free, mostly dishes like rice or quinoa that don’t need gluten rather than pale imitations of gluteny things. Green Chef even offers free phone consultation with a dietitian. (Korfhage’s counseled him on protein and fiber and directed me to the meals marked as consistent with the Mediterranean diet.).

In a recent development, meals arrive well-organized, in mostly recyclable packaging. Recipes are easy to follow, though the instructions are a bit minimalist. (Read ahead, and your prep times will go down.) The proteins are flavorful. And options are international and sophisticated, from shrimp spiced with Yemeni schug to cumin-ancho meat dishes. Even in August, the most difficult time to ship perishable food, herbs and veggies had nary a wilted leaf—a difficult and rare achievement, especially for fresh herbs like the parsley in the gremolata for a Turkish-spiced steelhead trout. Overall, there are fewer options than you’ll find from HelloFresh’s flagship kit, and Green Chef is among the more expensive meal kits. But the quality and variety of ingredients reflect that.

Hungryroot has among the lowest prep times of any meal kit we’ve tested that isn’t actually pre-prepped—perfect for the friend who “doesn’t have time to cook” and instead finds their DoorDash budget ballooning. Hungryroot meals tend to take about the same amount of time to cook as to eat, 10 to 20 minutes for most meals we’ve tried.

In a recent development, each meal tends to be assembled from a small number of components, with a lot of the prep already done. An organic sauce or salsa or dressing, some version of pre-mixed salad, a sprig of broccoli, a pack of sous-vide chicken or smoked pulled pork. It’s a bit like running a personal fast-casual restaurant out of your home kitchen.

It’s also nice that you can customize Hungryroot to suit your needs and dietary preferences. The substantial idea behind Hungryroot is to be a full-service, AI-assisted food concierge. First, Hungryroot logs all your dietary, lifestyle, and budget preferences. (Hate a mushroom? Follow a low-salt diet? Don’t like masala spices, specifically? Don’t worry.) Then it suggests a whole world of ingredients and recipes, which you can sub out from a seemingly endless list each week, depending on local ingredient availability. Usually, there’s room left over in the plan to add some fresh fruit or a sweet treat. One detriment of this ultra-customized system is that you’ve got to get pretty far through the ordering process (and enter your credit card) before seeing your personal menu. Here’s the online “cookbook” of potential menus, for those who’d like an early glimpse.

This is a bit of a game-changer for meal kits, frankly, though the scenario I just described would end up a bit expensive ($10 a serving, plus $10 shipping). And so Blue Apron also has a DoorDash-style loyalty model: Blue Apron Plus. You pay $10 a month—the price of shipping on a single order—and then shipping is free for the month. This means that if you order more than once a month, you save money by signing up. Price per meal has fanned out since the reboot, ranging from $8 a serving for lunchtime salads and wraps to $13 for hearty bakes and seafood plates. This lets you choose meals based on your budget.

Recent findings suggest that this is an ambitious turnaround for a meal kit that WIRED reviewers had loved in the past before going through some bumps in the road under upcoming ownership beginning in 2023. So far we’ve had pretty good results. Our most recent test included fun, internationalized recipes like crisp, lightly spicy bang bang chicken; bao bun burgers with shishito peppers; za’atar-spiced salmon; and an excellent, hearty shrimp and feta bake. Prep for most recipes hovered around 30 minutes. And on each, you could sub out a main protein. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck tried Blue Apron’s low-effort, assemble-and-bake meals and came away mostly impressed by the sourcing and ingredient quality—but also wondered whether the focus on simplicity led to compromises in some recipes. She couldn’t bring herself to bake raw meat for a harissa beef dish, per instructions, without first draining the grease. And so she cooked it in a skillet first.

There’d been a few ingredient hiccups in 2025 as the new initiative rolled out, but this summer Blue Apron partnered with grocery delivery service Misfits Market as a new fulfillment and delivery partner—theoretically leading to more regional options and faster delivery. Blue Apron has also changed its packaging to be more eco-friendly. As this goes fully online, we’ll retest Blue Apron to see the results. Note that beyond main proteins, allergens and dietary restrictions can be a little difficult to navigate on Blue Apron’s site.

With most aims at $7 a serving plus shipping, HelloFresh’s budget option, EveryPlate, remains the lowest-cost meal kit we've tested. And yet, this budget meal kit still uses the same proteins from local purveyors as HelloFresh’s much more expensive initiative.

It has been revealed that the secret is not skimping on calories or portions, but rather simplicity. EveryPlate’s meals derive their flavors from a small set of ingredients, and a single sauce or herb or spice mix—or perhaps some citrus cross-utilized as both juice and zest. Ingredients also tend to be cross-utilized quite a bit, which doubles as good cooking.

In a test this year, Korfhage made himself a fun Tex-Mex-style “quesabirria” with a chili-style spice paste; a hearty plate of pork chops with thyme and shallots; and a ground-turkey rice bowl that relied on ginger, garlic, and a mix of soy glaze and citric ponzu sauce.

HelloFresh’s low price makes it the only meal initiative we’ve tried that wouldn’t require any particular adjustment in a grocery budget—at least for two people. And yet, this budget meal plan from HelloFresh somehow offers dinners that even your judgy mom-in-law would recognize as balanced.

Industry observers note that this year’s pork chop meal, in particular, is the sort of meat-and-two supper you probably took for granted as a child. Pan-seared chops. Crispy-leafed Brussels sprouts baked in the oven. Fresh mashed potatoes. But what elevated the meal from basic staple to weekday extravagance was a thoughtful shallot-garlic-cream pan sauce, cooked with fresh thyme in the juices from the pork after finishing searing. The sauce was rich, complex, and aromatic.

The laundry list of staples you’re expected to have in your fridge for EveryPlate is a little longer than with more expensive kits, which includes flour and eggs. The box of ingredients is not as organized as HelloFresh’s. The menu is significantly shorter than HelloFresh’s at about 35 options, but still competitive with many meal delivery services. While the meals skew more basic than adventurous, EveryPlate impressed us with its simple, good taste and economy, at a price that wouldn’t stretch many household budgets.

Recent findings suggest that WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins, who eats no meat, had a good experience with EveryPlate's shorter menu of vegetarian options this past spring and secured a week’s worth of food for less than she ends up spending on groceries in Upcoming York City. Sure, you may want to fill out a meal by adding your own rice to supplement Korean-inflected beef or pork with squash and carrots. (A great rice cooker makes this easy.) It still adds up to an economical meal, one you might appreciate on a Tuesday when you’re out of other ideas.

Recent findings suggest that best budget meal delivery service for large families: Marley Spoon’s lower-cost meal kit, Dinnerly, was WIRED’s former budget pick. It’s still a good, affordable pick for small families, if not quite as low-cost as EveryPlate. But for large families (six portions), it’s almost certainly the best budget option at just $6 a meal (for six servings), with a much larger recipe selection. Compared to Korfhage’s testing last year, Dinnerly’s recipes have grown lighter, more sophisticated, and maybe a little smarter: a za'atar chicken recipe here, a Mediterranean-inflected pork tenderloin or lemon-butter shrimp there. Often it feels like you’re getting our top-pick kit, Marley Spoon, at a discount. The difference indicates up mostly in Dinnerly’s simpler ingredient list, usually featuring a single herb or spice accent rather than a complicated medley of flavors.

Of all the plant-based meal kits WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins has tried, Purple Carrot took the, uh, carrot. Purple Carrot offers boxes filled with premade, frozen, oven-ready meals—with adventurous dishes like mole enchiladas or an artichoke-stuffed ravioli that needed a little extra seasoning. But where Purple Carrot truly shines is with its fresh-made recipes. Unlike some meal kits that make you hunt through a box, the ingredients for each of Purple's recipes arrive well organized in individual plastic bags, accompanied by beautifully designed recipe cards. It’s also a flexible strategy: Order what you’d like each week, with a minimum $50 order.

Sources indicate that purple’s recipes are devoted to the joy of cooking—sometimes to a fault, as with some hour-long recipe preps. (Advertised shorter prep times, as is often the way with meal kit recipes, were bald-faced lies.) Higgins, a natural cook, loved the time spent sautéeing, searing, mixing, and spicing. She especially enjoyed the results. A lovely Mediterranean rice salad with stuffed grape leaves took just a half hour to make, with some simple oven-roasted radishes, grape tomatoes, and zucchini.

The results are a parade of textures as tasty as one would expect at a restaurant, but with relatively little effort, Higgins notes. Another meal of squash dumplings required boiling the squash and individually stuffing the dumplings, which took more than an hour. It ended up being Higgins’s favorite meal of the week, a case where effort meets reward. But the effort was nonetheless real. Purple Carrot bursts with texture, flavor, fun international ingredients, and the spirit of invention. If you’re the sort who likes to take time in the kitchen, there’s vegan gold at the end of that rainbow. Lately, Purple Carrot has also branched out into special meals, like a box designed in collaboration with fitness influencer Robin Arzón.

According to everyone we talked to who’s taking GLP-1 medication for weight loss or diabetes management, the drive to seek out delicious food just isn’t what it used to be. What has not changed is the utilitarian need to get enough protein, in a reasonable form, balanced against other health considerations. Does this not sound romantic? It mostly isn’t. But if hunger doesn’t move you like it used to, it’s even more important that your food tastes good enough to actually want to eat it.

According to recent reports, enter Tempo by Home Chef, a never-frozen, prepared meal service that offers about 30 meals each week. As many as two-thirds of these meals are marked “protein-packed,” with more than 30 grams of protein. And at least 10 of these are GLP-1-balanced, per a dietitian. What you’ll get: sufficient protein, not too many carbs, no other funny stuff.

Tempo’s proteins are well-managed, if unexciting. But the meals were easy, nutritious, balanced, and comforting, without relying on a pile of unhealthy sodium and carbs to be palatable. At $12 a meal, Tempo’s pricing is about par for the course for prepared meals.

Recent findings suggest that WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, who tested the GLP-1-balanced meals, found the portions appropriate for those on the medication and appreciated that the meals offered her the proteins she needs to maintain muscle mass even while chemically un-hungry. Just note: You may end up with a lot of chicken and a lot of fish. Both Merck and Korfhage were happy to see the occasional chicken thigh, and not just breast. Thighs are better tasting, for the record.

For pure protein-loading and macro management, a no-nonsense option is Fuel Meals (see below), which has almost no sodium and more than 40 grams of protein per meal.

These meal kits former WIRED reviewer and lead tester Matthew Korhage tried didn’t make his final cut, but he still recommends them. Here are his thoughts on what he liked and what held them back.

In a recent development, sunbasket (~$16 per serving): Sunbasket focuses heavily on fresh, organic ingredients and offers a whole lot of variety in its menus. Its recipes are attentive to saucing and to basic good cooking techniques such as deglazing. Like Hungryroot, it also offers breakfasts and snacks to supplement meal options with little extras such as coconut yogurt and sous-vide egg bites. The meal kit also lets you filter out allergen-containing items. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved the flexibility and add-ons. During a recent test, I enjoyed an excellent Greek chicken and orzo salad dish—and, wonder of wonders, the advertised prep time was actually the actual prep time (about 30 minutes). The focus on organic ingredients does make Sunbasket one of the more expensive meal kit options, and the annual Thanksgiving meal kit has remained a lovely and welcome extravagance at $200.

According to recent reports, gardencup ($11 to $15 a serving): Gardencup is a little like having the whole menu of Sweetgreen sent to your house or office, except in cylindrical form. Basically, you pick out premade salads, soups, and snacks, and they come in little cups—fresh, lovely, crisp, and ready to eat. I found it to be a great way to keep myself eating healthy when there’s no time to cook at the office (or the home office), which is typically when DoorDash or freezer-meal temptations run wild. It remains among the healthiest prepared food delivery options I know. I even tested Gardencup as a salad option during a cyclospora parasite scare, in part because I missed salad and because Gardencup could attest that it did not use lettuce from any of the suspected sources of the outbreak. The salads remained delicious and delivered a shocking amount of protein in the meat options. But variety of options is not a strong suit. A slackened focus on local sourcing, plus limited transparency on sourcing—Gardencup will disclose only that it sources its greens in the salad belt from Salinas, California, to Yuma, Arizona—has kept Gardencup in my honorable mentions.

Factor ($13 to $17 a serving): Factor is a prepared-meal delivery plan run by HelloFresh, with ready-to-eat meals that look a lot like TV dinners. But there’s a twist: The trays have never been frozen. They were made fresh in a commissary kitchen and shipped with cold packs, so they taste kind of like restaurant leftovers. Consistently, Factor ranks among the best-tasting prepared meal plans I’ve tested, especially when I shrug off the directions and reheat my meals in an air fryer instead of a microwave. Proteins and high-protein meals are a strong suit. Proteins maintain their texture quite well, especially a truffled filet mignon I couldn’t believe I microwaved. Still, some meals, especially carb-avoidant or keto meals, are oddly mushy, while meals centered on proteins and whole starches, like potatoes or rice, alongside veggies like green beans or Brussels sprouts, tended to fare quite well. So did stir-fry-style meals. My gluten-free colleague, Scott Gilbertson, wrote that he had the best luck with Factor’s Mexican fare. I do wish Factor would shed its reliance on the microwave: When I went off-script and used a Ninja Crispi air fryer or convection oven, I had much better results than with the nuker. But non-air-fryer ovens do not seem to offer the same improvement. Like many ready-to-eat meals, it’s a bit more expensive than the kits you cook yourself. Oh, and as a bonus? Factor has a really, truly delicious selection of nutrient-amped juice bottles and elderberry “shots.” I could pretty much subsist on their probiotic cucumber-pineapple green juice.

According to recent reports, fuel Meals ($14 to $15 a serving): Fuel Meals are a no-nonsense, no-fluff, no-added-ingredients, pure-protein-packed nutritive meal blueprint, with many meals paleo-friendly. Some of Fuel’s meals had as few as five ingredients, essentially the macronutrients plus a modicum of oil and salt. A large percentage of meals are marked gluten-free or dairy-free. Does all this mean less flavor? It can. The meals are also often not beautiful, dominated by a large and no-fuss serving of protein. But Fuel’s meal service offers an admirable focus, especially for those bulking up or watching carbs. Meals are substantive, usually topping 600 calories and 40 grams of protein, with no added sugar, fatty dairy, or carb-heavy filler. As a baby gym rat, I appreciate how clear the macros are, but some meals are high in sodium and often aren’t deficit-friendly.

In a recent development, wildgrain ($13 to $17 per loaf or box of pastries): This is less a meal delivery service than a way to step up a home meal. Wildgrain is a monthly bread-box delivery: You receive par-baked bread and pastries from small bakeries across the country. This is pretty much the same process that likely happens at local restaurants when your warm bread basket comes out: It’s not quite as high-quality as you’d get directly from an artisan bakery, if you live in places with artisan bakeries. But it’s also as fresh as it gets, and I had a great experience testing the box in October 2025, especially the sourdough breads, which are perfect for large meals with houseguests. You finish baking at home, so you end up with ultra-fresh bread, biscuits, doughnuts, or scones that are still warm and crisp from the oven. A Wildgrain subscription arrives as a monthly box filled with four, six, or 12 items, ranging from a full sourdough loaf or fresh-made pasta to a pack of six doughnuts or four large croissants. Basically, you build your own box each month, choosing from healthy sourdough or pasta and decadent pastries.

Thistle ($12 to $15 per meal): A prior top pick for solo diners with individually prepared dishes that require little to no prep, Thistle is mostly a plant-based meal kit—but you can add sustainable meats to any otherwise vegan meal for $3. It’s also so local and seasonal that the West and East Coasts have different menus, and the whole middle of the country, except Chicago, gets none. (You can check your zip code here to see if you can get delivery.) Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So used Thistle to get herself to eat more vegetables and thus avoid a life of rickets and/or scurvy. Portions are generous enough to split among meals, and in a nice turn for those who hate disposing of boxes, Thistle's drivers will pick up the cooler bag that held last week’s meal and replace it with a new one full of food. WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins’s favorite meals from Thistle were a whirlwind of textures, including a Mexican-inspired corn and poblano chile salad with adobo pinto beans and a chilled, lemongrass-accented rice noodle bowl that mixed spice, tang, crisp veggies, and deep umami from mushrooms and seaweed. She still dreams about it sometimes. Breakfasts are available at a lower cost, as low as $9.

It has been revealed that tovala (~$9 to $15 a serving): It’s not every day you get to try something that feels super fresh. Tovala offers perhaps the most ambitious ready-to-heat and prepared-meal delivery solution I’ve seen: the meal kits come with an oven! Unlike the sogginess of many prepared meals, Tovala's recipes come in little foil pans with recipes custom-designed for a small steam oven. The results are often delicious—as was the case during my testing with a sweet chili–glazed salmon with pickled veg and noodles—and the QR code scanning function makes each recipe seamless to cook. Stick with the meal initiative for six weeks, and you get a quite affordable and powerful little convection oven, toaster, and steamer. A previous flaw was that Tovala only offered single-serve meals. But as of early 2026, at least four or five meals a week offer two to four servings, making the meal delivery service much more useful to families and couples—and much more economical per serving. But note that it’s also one of the most sodium-filled meal services I’ve tested.

According to recent reports, gobble ($17 a serving): Formerly the top pick for fast-cooked meals, Gobble previously wowed with speed-demon dishes that also offered interesting and worldly flavors. Indeed, the most recent test included Caribbean rondon, an Indonesian peanut curry stir-fry, and steak vierge. But while the flavors have stayed interesting, the focus on fast cooking appears to have waned since my colleague Louryn Strampe tested Gobble. Cook time estimates aren’t printed on the recipe cards, but meals took as long as 30 minutes. For now, Hungryroot has taken the fast-cooking crown. For small households, Gobble is also among the most expensive kits. At most portions, prices approach $17 a serving plus shipping.

Sources indicate that nurture Life ($6 to $7 per serving): Nurture Life is like a restaurant kids’ menu in ready-to-eat meal-kit form. We loved the idea behind this fresh-made, never-frozen delivery meal plan when we tested it a few years back: toddler- and slightly bigger kid-friendly meals, from mac and cheese to spaghetti and meatballs to myriad variations on the chicken nugget. Meal prices have dipped to reasonable levels lately, so it's likely due for a retest—and each plate includes vegetables alongside the greatest hits.

Veestro ($7 to $14 per serving): WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe enjoyed Veestro as a ready-to-eat vegan option, with premade meals delivered fresh and freezable for extra meals on hand in a pinch. The service offers a number of filters for other dietary requirements, and satisfying taste and texture—which is not always a guarantee on ready-to-eat meals. Veestro has updated its menu and offerings since the last time WIRED tested, including several snacky soup offerings. The online menu interface, which lets you sort by ingredients and filter out unwanted ones, is among the best I’ve seen.

Sources indicate that splendid Spoon ($9 to $13 per serving): Splendid Spoon is a nutrition delivery kit that offers plant-based smoothies, soups, bowls, noodles, and shots. Everything here is natural and free of gluten or GMOs, including spaghetti and plant-based “meatballs.” WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe has a big yen for the smoothies in particular ($10 apiece), but wasn’t quite prepared for the intensity of a lemon juice shot that comes as part of a five-pack of dense 3-ounce superfoods.

ModifyHealth’s Braised Beef (top) and Paprika Salmon (bottom).

ModifyHealth ($10 to $13 per serving): The idea behind ModifyHealth is that food can be medicine. Sometimes, I’ll admit, it tasted like it was designed purely for nutrition rather than flavor. ModifyHealth is a prepared meal delivery service tailored to people who need a heart-healthy, low-carb, or low-FODMAP diet to avoid dire digestive or health consequences. GLP-1 weight-loss aims are also available for people with diabetes or others. Gluten-free meals are attested to be made in an entirely gluten-free facility. The meals were simple, benign, and low-sodium but also sometimes a little soggy—a common problem with prepared meals. The plastic top of the packaging was also difficult to disengage from the base of each meal tray—a problem when the plastic is hot after a turn in the microwave. But here’s what I do like: The meals are carefully tailored with consultation from dietitians to help people for whom food can be a source of fear or pain. Many insurance plans cover an additional service: one-on-one dietitian consultation. ModifyHealth also offers a free consultation for those just trying to figure out which diet strategy is right for them. For those with IBS in particular, this remains the most focused food plan I’ve seen.

Recent findings suggest that daily Harvest (prices vary): Daily Harvest is another ready-to-eat meal delivery service specializing in dietary restrictions: plant-based, plus gluten- and dairy-free. Smoothies are a highlight, as are harvest bowls, pastas, and grains. Calories are low. Ingredients are often inventive. The meal’s a lifesaver for the solo vegan eater without time to prep a meal, and WIRED’s Molly Higgins appreciated that the meals mostly relied on the natural flavors of the vegetables themselves, accented with flavors like curry and lemongrass. As with many frozen meals, however, texture wasn't a strong suit. The ready-to-blend smoothies are great, though.

Sakara Life ($30+ per serving): Sakara Life offers plant-based weekly menus in fresh, prepared portions, with greens, flavorful sauces, all-organic ingredients, and textural add-ons like seeds or berries. But it’s among the most expensive meal plans we’ve tested, and neither WIRED reviewer who tried it really cottoned to it. Louryn Strampe questioned the science behind detox and cleanse health claims, calling Sakara “egregiously expensive” and full of “bitter veggies and tart fruits.” Molly Higgins, meanwhile, remarked Sakara Life’s tinctures and metabolism supplements didn’t agree with her system, and that the mostly raw-food initiative made her long for “human food.”.

Are Meal Delivery Services Worth It?

According to recent reports, if you're talking raw materials by the pound—meat, zucchini, rice, noodles—meal kits will, of course, cost more than buying food at grocery stores. It's a service, after all, with added value above simple ingredient cost. Unless you've got quite expensive taste, you'll easily be able to make delicious meals at home for less than the $7 to $14 a serving that a meal kit will cost. That said, this doesn't necessarily mean that meal kits are expensive for what they offer. We conducted an experiment, trying to re-create four different meal-kit meals by going to my local grocery store—buying every ingredient provided by the meal kit. Turns out, if you don't have the right sauces and spices at home already, it's very difficult to re-create these tasty meals at grocery stores for less than they cost from a meal kit, in part because you'll most likely have to buy full containers of sauces and spices instead of preportioned ingredients,.

So, is HelloFresh worth it compared to a grocery store? Caveats are in order: For staple ingredients and spices you'll use in multiple recipes, the grocery store is, of course, cheaper. Once you buy a container of paprika for an individual recipe, it will also be there for future recipes, whereas meal-kit spices are portioned for the meal. So the real answer is that meal kits can be a quite economical way of trying out a fresh recipe, or a new style of cooking, without larding up your fridge with condiments you won't use again. For ingredients you'd use less commonly, a meal kit can reduce waste and spoilage, and maybe even compete on price for an individual meal.

If your comparison point is takeout, well, the best meal delivery services on this list will almost certainly be cheaper and more nutritious. We've found that a meal kit in the fridge tends to be a good motivator to cook a nutritious meal—and thus can save both the money and the cholesterol.

It has been revealed that to really save on cost, some people like to keep testing out the trial offers and discounts. Much like mattress-in-a-box companies, meal kit companies usually have a running promotion. Usually this takes the form of a trial discount price that'll drop your cost by half or more on the first box, in hopes you'll like the service enough to keep it on at full price.

A meal kit a few times a week ends up balancing out well: It's a motivating factor to eat better, and it means that when you do go to the grocery store, you can do so less mindlessly and more purposefully, given that you've got a few meals' worth of ingredients in the fridge. It's also had the side effect of broadening your culinary toolkit, keeping you from getting stuck in the same ruts.

It has been revealed that that stated, it's a set grocery expense and not necessarily a small one. Tossing or recycling cold packs and boxes gets tiring. And depending on the time of year, you may prefer shopping in person for what's seasonal and local, when produce is at its peak—an experience you don't get from a meal kit, or from grocery delivery, for that matter. If you're cooking for a bigger household, meal kits can also lose their utility quite quickly. A convenient option for two can become a much larger expense for a family of four or six.

Can I Pause a Meal Kit Service When I Go on Vacation?

Pretty much every meal kit tested has an option to pause subscriptions—and there's no particular limit to how often you can do this. The main thing is to be sure that you've canceled with enough lead time. Some services let you cancel or pause delivery as late as the Friday before a Monday delivery. HelloFresh requires five days' notice. Marley Spoon requires six days, based on one of our testers’ home locations. Some, like Hungryroot, may lock in next week's order as early as the previous Monday, depending on where you live. Read your terms of service, and act accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that for those with more variable schedules, the service we'd probably recommend is Blue Apron, which changed its model last year and no longer locks in delivery each week. You'll have to remember to order a box each week, which can be done where I am with four days' notice.

According to recent reports, don't order too many meals per week: You know the old John Lennon line: Life is what happens when you're busy, out eating a random burrito, then thinking guiltily about the meal kit at home in your fridge. Aspirations are great, but don't order more meals than you're likely to make, or you'll be sad. Err on the side of caution. Order just enough meals per week that making yourself a recipe from your HelloFresh or Home Chef box is still a delight and a convenience and an overall boon to your life—not an obligation. If you're somewhat improvisational and impulsive, three meals a week is the sweet spot. The prospect of a few easy meals usually saves me from an impulse weeknight DoorDash.

Make room in your fridge: Meal kits take the place of a lot of grocery shopping. But they're also a lot of food, and a lot to keep organized. Clear a tall enough space in the fridge to put the whole meal kit box in, after pulling out the cold packs: This way, you're not left worrying about which groceries belong to the meal kit, and you won't lose any ingredients. You can just pull the whole box out when you want to make a meal. That remarked, some plans like Home Chef, HelloFresh, and Green Chef are very good at organizing each meal into its own separate bag. An added bonus from these more organized plans is that you'll be able to use less space in your fridge. Over time, this will matter.

Recent findings suggest that check the recipe cards to make sure you have everything you need to make a recipe: Most meal kits expect that you'll have certain staple ingredients in your home, usually including oil and butter. Recipes also have requirements for cookware. Check this before you start a recipe. Nothing worse than realizing you need a stick of butter on step 5, with carrots already browning in the oven.

According to recent reports, remember, you owe nothing to the recipe: Meal kit services hire recipe developers, and on the best meal kits, these chefs have spent a lot of time optimizing each recipe. But you owe them nothing—nothing! Add spices, change steps, season food when you want to season it. Meal kits can teach you a lot about how to make a good meal and shake you out of tired culinary routines. But it's your meal. Make it how you like. Have fun.

Industry observers note that chances are, whatever time of the year, a WIRED reviewer is testing a meal kit. We constantly cycle through various meal kits, testing and retesting each of our top picks at least once a year—and often multiple times, especially when each meal delivery service changes its format or expands to latest offerings.

When possible, we order at least four meals a week from each meal delivery service. We prepare meals according to instructions and see how well they go. If we deviate from instructions out of horror or curiosity or a simple sense of culinary propriety, we note this and tell you why.

According to recent reports, we check prep times against what's advertised (rarely an exercise in honesty!) and take note of any inconsistencies, vagueness, or frustration in the recipe card instructions. Convenience matters: If a meal kit needlessly recommends a nonstick pan, we like it less—especially if the recipe indicates to heat that pan before adding food, or later mentions browned fond. Nonstick isn’t cast iron or carbon; there’s no fond. If rice portions are too small, we'll flag that.

Sources indicate that the quality and freshness of the produce are important, and the same goes for the meat. Where possible, we look into where the meat was sourced, and check on the reputation, safety, and standards of the meat suppliers. If a meal kit swears it's gluten-free, we verify this—calling certifying organizations where relevant.

It has been revealed that we usually try to order as varied a menu as possible. We might check in on gluten-free meals, a seafood item, a vegetarian item, and white and dark meat items. We might also test a Midwestern-style hot dish or Southern meat-and-two alongside meals that draw (or attempt to draw) from global inspirations. Sometimes we test the same meal kit multiple times for different dietary needs, or call in multiple testers to do so. WIRED's vegan tester, Molly Higgins, often tests the same meal kit as lead tester Matthew Korfhate does, but with a different focus.

Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard.
  • Recent findings suggest that members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

It has been revealed that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Recent findings suggest that members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

Industry observers note that "Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," said Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

The discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

It has been revealed that most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

According to recent reports, the barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

According to recent reports, rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Industry observers note that once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

It has been revealed that the clear, gelatinous covering serves another notable purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

In a recent development, scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

Industry observers note that ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

According to recent reports, "Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," remarked Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

In a recent development, the rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two key firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

Sources indicate that MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)

‘Blade Runner 2099’ cast praise the incredible set designs that brought the sci-fi universe to life: ‘it was all so well-realized’ (interview)

  • Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Video’s "Blade Runner 2099" has arrived with an 8-episode limited series revealing what the "Blade Runner" world looks like 50 years after the events of director Denis Villeneuve’s "Blade Runner 2049.".

The most obvious change in this depressing dystopia is that replicants are running the LA show after some unmentionable ecological disaster and humans are now the ones relegated to underclass citizens.

Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.

We connected with three of the sci-fi show’s main co-stars, Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon"), Lewis Gribben ("T2 Trainspotting") and Dimitri Abold ("Love Addicts") to hear more about working with creator/showrunner Silka Louisa, and immersing themselves in "Blade Runner 2099's" vivid futuristic worldbuilding.

"For me it's a lot simpler than egos because he's such a goal-oriented person and all of his stuff has such a police procedural quality to it," Needham tells SPACE regarding his role as Yahya, an emotionless replicant who despises all humans.

According to recent reports, "It was really fun to just follow what Silka [Louisa] did. She wrote this great, really exciting mystery thriller, and I just got to play in that.”.

Scottish actor Gribben portrays Cora's ailing younger brother Elias, who has compromised mobility and a rocky relationship with his overprotective sister.

"I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television demonstrates. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it.".

It has been revealed that as Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character.

"Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. "Starting out as someone who’s so hopeful and has to try and scrape up the last dregs of hope as things start falling apart. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for.".

"Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations feature detailed production design that allowed the actors to experience a seamless transition into the complex shoot.

"For me and Dimitri, our first day was in Bebeto’s apartment, and it was all so well-realized,” Gribben recalls.

"You saw all the gadgets because obviously Bebeto was a bit of a tinkerer of a character and had lots of machinery and works and stuff. It took up about 70% of the acting, and we just had to come with compelling conviction. It made it so easy. When you audition for these things, you feel like you have to act more because you’re in a blue screen vacuum. But then you’re there, and it’s so visually well created like that, it made it so easy to be immersed in it.".

"Blade Runner 2099" is currently airing all 8 episodes exclusively on Prime Video.

Hims & Hers launches newly introduced peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it announced the latest products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • It has been revealed that the upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the latest products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

It has been revealed that the upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October introduced an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a organization spokesperson said in a statement.

Sources indicate that none of the manufacturer's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims stated they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

It has been revealed that the company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

According to recent reports, hims noted it prepares to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized initiative to their needs, if appropriate.

The company mentioned it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

Recent findings suggest that "If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori remarked there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

According to recent reports, "We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he remarked. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a organization of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He stated Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, remarked Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

But he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

Recent findings suggest that that appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The firm claims patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In a recent development, in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

It has been revealed that HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "big fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

Sources indicate that there is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data demonstrates only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione revealed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also noted in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Falkirk and Rangers meet for a second time this season.

The Scottish Premiership rolls into town again this weekend with crucial games in both halves of the table.

Last week, Falkirk beat St Johnstone to secure six top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1966.

Victory at Ibrox on Saturday would make it seven in a row in the highest Scottish league for the first time since 1907, during a season in which the Bairns finished second.

In order to do that, John McGlynn's side would have to become the first Falkirk team to win against Rangers at Ibrox since a 1994 League Cup tie when Richard Cadette scored twice in a 2-1 victory.

Falkirk are also looking to hold on to third place, with Hearts a point behind having played a game fewer.

However, Rangers have their own motivation, not least extending their 14-match unbeaten run in all competitions - a sequence that has included 12 wins.

By winning their game in hand against Aberdeen on Tuesday, Rangers moved to within a point of Premiership leaders and reigning champions Celtic.

Therefore, three points would take Rangers top before Celtic visit Hearts on Sunday.

Highlights: Rangers 3-2 Aberdeen.

According to recent reports, two games in, Mario Frick's reign as Aberdeen head coach has produced 11 goals - six for, five against - and one win and one loss. Heavy metal football, as he promised.

Both were away from home - against Kilmarnock and Rangers - and on Saturday, Frick takes charge of a game at Pittodrie for the first time, with Dundee the visitors.

The Dons have won just twice at home in the Premiership this season, their last such victory coming in mid-October.

Dundee are still licking their wounds after last Saturday's 8-0 home defeat by Hearts and Tuesday's 2-1 loss away to Hibs.

Steven Pressley's side are on a three-match losing run after a promising start to the season.

Though they are not in any immediate danger of being dragged down towards the relegation zone, such a scenario may not be far away unless they arrest their current slide.

Highlights: Hibernian 2-1 Dundee.

Four points separate St Johnstone in sixth and second bottom Motherwell.

Dundee are just below Saints on goal difference while three teams - Aberdeen, Hibernian and St Mirren - are a point above Well.

It's so tight and bottom side Kilmarnock, who visit St Mirren, are four points adrift and at risk of becoming detached.

This weekend's fixtures could make the order of the bottom seven look rather different come close of play on Saturday.

St Johnstone are away to fifth-placed Dundee United, but Aberdeen v Dundee, St Mirren v Kilmarnock and the evening meeting of Motherwell and Hibs at Fir Park pitch those congested sides up against one another.

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran.

Celtic took only one point from last season's trips to Tynecastle but had the last laugh with victory over Hearts in Glasgow on the final day of the league season to tip Derek McInnes' side to the Premiership title.

McInnes' replacement Wouter Vrancken took his much-changed Hearts side to Celtic Park last month and were overrun in a 7-1 defeat, easily Celtic's best performance of the season so far.

Sunday is a chance for Hearts to atone for that loss and give Vrancken the sort of statement performance and win the home supporters are looking for.

Both sides had European fixtures on Thursday, with varying results.

Hearts were undone by a late goal in their 3-2 Conference League defeat at home to Monaco before Celtic boosted their hopes of Europa League progress with a 2-1 victory away to Portuguese side Torreense.

European hangovers notwithstanding, any goals would ensure an extension of no 0-0 draws between these sides since 2015.
